title: Ameen Nayfeh's 'Jo of Montreal': A Rare Feel-Good Family Film from West Asia
summary:
Ameen Nayfeh, the award-winning director of the Palestinian drama '200 Meters,' has taken a surprising turn with his new film, 'Jo of Montreal.' It's a feel-good family film about Yusuf, a spoiled 12-year-old boy who visits family in Jordan and gets stranded in a remote village. After forming an unlikely bond with Abu Khalil, a retired teacher-turned-shepherd, Yusuf rediscovers his roots and develops a passion for the community's ancient heritage and its famous crusader-era castle known as Montreal.

Nayfeh had the idea for years, but it was after making '200 Meters' — about a Palestinian family separated by the wall dividing Israel from the Occupied Territories — that he felt the need to tell a story that would also appeal to younger viewers. His two young nieces appeared in '200 Meters' and were eager to watch it, but it's not exactly a film for children. He found it difficult to recommend films they could watch on their own. 'The inspiration came from the place, from the village and the castle,' he says. 'That's where I saw a great potential to tell a story from that region.'

The film follows Yusuf as he arrives in Shoubak feeling disconnected from his homeland and absorbed by his screen. A village rivalry leaves him stranded in the mountains, where Abu Khalil and his wife, Fatima, take him in. As Yusuf helps Abu Khalil with his historical reenactment and builds his public profile through social media, the three become an improvised family. When a development scheme threatens Abu Khalil's home and the old village, Yusuf brings together his former rivals to protect Montreal's heritage. Described as ''Theeb' meets 'The Karate Kid' — but with no karate,' the adventurous coming-of-age story is built around mentorship, belonging and the imagination of a young Arab boy.

Nayfeh approached producer Bassam Alasad of Dubai-based Creative Media Solutions, who happily agreed. 'We are both invested in telling a coming-of-age, feel-good movie because these stories don't really exist in the Arab world, in the Middle East,' Nayfeh says. 'The independent film scene is not interested in making films targeting kids.' Alasad adds, 'I love working on hopeful films, coming-of-age stories and films that have that kind of feel good vibe to them.'

Despite the success of '200 Meters,' Nayfeh initially experienced pushback. 'Actually it's something that we really struggled with - that I'm a Palestinian filmmaker. I should only make films about Palestine. That was told to us, to both of us as a team, in my face.' He also struggled with the question during the war in Gaza. 'The film was greenlit for production during the war on Gaza. And that was a very difficult time,' he says. 'But we wanted to make a feel-good film. I think it's important to me to make those stories because if we are only producing difficult films, hard films, tragedies, what are the younger generations going to watch? It's just to give them a small beacon of hope, a bit of entertainment.'

Shot on location in Jordan, at the site of Montreal castle near the town of Shoubak, as well as in Saudi Arabia, the production took place in the midst of the U.S. war against Iran, which caused major problems for the crew. Jordanian filmmaker Zain Duraie told Variety about a similar experience she had with Western funders when making her award-winning family drama 'Sink.' 'Unfortunately, there are some perceived notions about the Middle East and what they're expecting to see from this region,' says Alasad. 'Sometimes when the story is just a family driven story or a story about a very specific case of humanity, it's unexpected to be coming from this region. So we want to do films that we want to do. And we know that it has an audience.'
why_it_matters: The film's struggle to get made shows how global money shapes which stories from the Middle East reach screens: funders often expect tragedy or politics, leaving children's and family films badly under-served. If 'Jo of Montreal' succeeds, it could prove there is a market for young Arab audiences — and widen what the region is allowed to look like on film.

questions.correct_answer: 'Theeb' meets 'The Karate Kid' — but with no karate

background_read: Ameen Nayfeh is a Palestinian filmmaker whose 2020 feature '200 Meters' follows a father trying to reach a hospital on the other side of the barrier that Israel built through and around the West Bank; in 2004 the International Court of Justice — the United Nations' top court — advised that the barrier was contrary to international law.
That film won prizes at international festivals, and Nayfeh's young nieces appeared in it, which helps explain why he wanted to make something children could watch on their own.

The 'Montreal' of the title is Montreal Castle, also known as Shobak Castle — a Crusader fortress from the Middle Ages in southern Jordan near the town of Shoubak, the kind of site that draws historians and tourists.

The comparison to 'Theeb' points to a 2014 Jordanian film directed by Naji Abu Nowar that was nominated for an Academy Award and told a Bedouin boy's coming-of-age story in the desert, while 'The Karate Kid' (1984) is an American film about a boy mentored by an older man.

Independent cinema in the Arab world is small and depends heavily on European festivals, funds and co-producers, which tend to reward serious or political stories — one reason a feel-good children's film is unusual.

perspectives.description: For young Arab viewers, a big-screen adventure with an Arab boy at its centre is rare, and the story treats heritage and mentorship as things worth fighting for. Shooting on location in Jordan and Saudi Arabia also means jobs for regional crews, and the castle setting could draw visitors to the Shoubak area.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the pressure on Palestinian artists
perspectives.description: Some critics argue that a Palestinian director should be making films about Palestine, especially while the war in Gaza continues, and that a light family comedy can look out of touch. Nayfeh says exactly this pressure was put to him 'in my face' by people in the industry.

The film exposes how Middle Eastern cinema is financed: money usually comes from European festivals, funds and co-producers that favour serious, political or tragic stories, so children's films are commercially risky. Producer Bassam Alasad says Western funders hold 'perceived notions' about what stories this region should tell.

If the film finds an audience, it could open doors for other Arab directors who want to make hopeful, kid-friendly films, and encourage regional funds and streaming platforms to invest in them. If it doesn't, funders may fall back on the familiar tragedy template, narrowing the picture of the region that the world sees.
